title: Tuning correlated states in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene with magnetic encapsulation
summary: Rhombohedral graphene multilayers provide a flexible platform for correlated physics associated with their flat-band electronic structure. While a variety of correlated states appear in these systems as a function of bias and electrostatic doping, promoting specific correlated flavor symmetry breaking states remains a challenge. Here we show that magnetic encapsulation by CrGeTe3 achieves this in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene, by using switchable exchange couplings induced by ferromagnetic substrates. We show that correlations in rhombohedral multilayers at charge neutrality strongly renormalize the exchange proximity splitting,giving rise to collective spin modes whose character is switched by the parallel or antiparallel alignment of the encapsulation. We further show that upon doping of the flat bands, spin triplet f-wave superconducting solutions emerge, whose layer and spin selectivity is controlled by the magnetic encapsulation, hosting in-gap excitations at the edges. Our results establish magnetic alignment as a means to control spin symmetry breaking and unconventional superconductivity in rhombohedral pentalayer graphene.

title: The role of preparation protocols in the Mpemba effect under time-delayed Newton cooling
summary: The Mpemba effect depends on both the relaxation dynamics and the protocol used to prepare the initial states. Here, this dependence is investigated using the time-delayed Newton cooling law, comparing protocols in which two samples are exposed to piecewise-constant bath temperatures before being placed in a common final bath. For protocols with at most two quenches and a common waiting time, exact conditions for the occurrence of the effect are derived. They rule out the Pontus protocol within this model and show that the synchronous two-reservoir protocol maximizes the effect magnitude within the class considered. The robustness of this optimum is then examined by allowing asynchronous quenches or an additional quench for one sample. Numerical optimization of these extensions identifies the synchronous two-reservoir protocol as the maximizing limit in the cases studied. This evidence motivates a conjecture that the same protocol remains optimal for more general bath histories, although that broader statement is not proved.

title: Discrete time crystals stabilized by bounded measurement noise
summary: Periodically driven clean interacting systems generically heat up, which destroys discrete time-crystalline order. Here we ask whether continuous weak measurement can stabilize such order. We study a long-range interacting spin chain whose local occupation is continuously monitored. Measurements generally induce a transition from volume-law to area-law entanglement. Yet low entanglement alone is not enough: along typical quantum trajectories, the system still reaches a featureless state with no subharmonic response. In contrast, the most-probable trajectory, obtained by suppressing measurement fluctuations, shows robust period doubling. To connect these limits, we introduce a bounded-noise protocol that restricts measurement fluctuations to a finite window. Narrow windows preserve period doubling. Intermediate windows produce coexisting time-crystalline and non-time-crystalline trajectories. Over time, trajectories leave the time-crystalline group one by one, so the order is long lived but finite. Wide windows destroy the order. Our results establish bounded measurement noise, discarding the large-deviation trajectories, as a route to time-crystalline order in clean systems. They also show that the measurement-induced area-law phase is necessary, but not sufficient, for this order.

title: Gate-tunable supercurrent switching in a three-terminal quantum dot transistor
summary: We propose and analyze a three-terminal superconducting transistor switch in which a gate-defined quantum dot region interrupts a flux-controlled loop. The output supercurrent is switched off completely when the two loop arms couple to the dot with equal tunneling strengths and half a flux quantum threads the loop. The device then operates as a symmetric SQUID at half flux. The condition follows from a single geometric factor $\chi$, which reduces the three-terminal problem to an equivalent two-terminal Anderson impurity model and makes the switching mechanism independent of the Coulomb interaction, the dot level position, the total hybridization and temperature. These enter only through a prefactor and thus decide how tolerant the device is to imperfect barrier tuning. Numerical renormalization group calculations across the full coupling parameter space show that the resonance is embedded in a broad region of elevated switching ratio at intermediate hybridization $\Gamma \approx \Delta$, while both weaker and stronger coupling reduce it to a thin isolated line. Finite temperature smooths the underlying singlet-doublet transition and lowers the supercurrent amplitude, but affects the open and closed states comparably and leaves the switching ratio largely intact. Within a zero-bandwidth two-level model, a second dot level is shown to open a leakage channel that grows as the two levels approach in energy. Raising the output barrier and the realistic presence of inter-level Coulomb repulsion, however, suppress the leakage.

title: Deriving Tsallis Entropy from First Principles
summary: The kinetic approach for q-distribution is extended through a "bottom-up" procedure to the corresponding entropic formula. In this way, the validity of Tsallis' formula, S_q(W) = k_B ln_q(W), is established from first principles. The resulting q-entropy is additive and the zeroth law of thermodynamics is automatically satisfied because the conventional identification beta = 1/(k_B T) remains valid. Entropy, energy, and all relevant quantities for both discrete and continuous cases are evaluated using standard (linear) averages. The "bottom-up" and "top-down" approaches yield the same q-distribution for velocities. The standard results are naturally recovered in the limit q -> 1.

title: Real Topology on Symmetry-Invariant Loops Enforces Superconducting Pairing Zeros
summary: Normal-state topology can obstruct superconducting pairing and give rise to gapless nodes in the quasiparticle spectrum. However, existing pairing-obstruction mechanisms largely rely on Fermi-surface topology or global Bloch-band topology. Here, we establish a new and general mechanism: one-dimensional (1D) real topology, defined on antiunitary-symmetry-invariant loops, enforces pairing zeros without requiring Fermi-surface or global Bloch-band topology. We derive sufficient conditions and lower bounds for pairing zeros across diverse pairing channels, for both zero and finite Cooper-pair momenta. The theorems apply to systems of arbitrary spatial dimensions without requiring the pairing bands to be globally isolated. We further show that such topologically enforced pairing zeros, if isolated, necessarily carry odd vorticity and can give rise to Bogoliubov-de Gennes nodes and zero-energy boundary modes, as demonstrated in a minimal two-orbital model. Our results reshape the understanding of how normal-state topology can obstruct the superconducting order, highlight the significant role of 1D real topology beyond single-particle band phenomena, and provide a general framework for identifying candidate materials hosting nodal superconductivity.

title: Revealing laser-induced modification of weak ferromagnetism through a spin-reorientation phase transition in iron borate Fe$_3$BO$_6$
summary: In the iron oxide Fe$_3$BO$_6$ weak ferromagnetism stems from competing contributions from two-site Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI) and from on-site anisotropies at the two $4c$ and $8d$ types of nonequivalent Fe$^{3+}$ sites. As a result, spin reorientation (SR) transition $\Gamma_2$ $\rightarrow$ $\Gamma_4$ in Fe$_3$BO$_6$ uniquely comprises 90$^\circ$ spin switching and a 35% change of weak ferromagnetic moment. We explore ultrafast kinetics of such a transition as a proxy for weak ferromagnetism contributions modified by femtosecond laser pulses. Using magneto-optical pump-probe technique we reveal that the SR transition is triggered by an abrupt decrease of the weak ferromagnetic moment in the $\Gamma_2$ phase, and relate it to the laser-induced modification of the DMI and anisotropy contributions to the spin canting. By tuning the pump pulse phonon energy between different optical absorption ranges, we show that laser-driven impact on spin canting possesses a nonthermal character and is achieved through the charge-transfer transitions $2p\rightarrow3d$ within Fe$^{3+}$O$^{2-}_6$ octahedra rather than by localized $3d\rightarrow3d$ transitions at Fe$^{3+}$. The decreased weak ferromagnetic moment controls the threshold and the latency of the SR transition, as well as a final state. The latter is achieved via the precessional switching to the $\Gamma_4$ phase activated by the laser-induced heating. Final state is found to be a coexistence of $\Gamma_4$ and $\Gamma_2$ phase with modified spin canting persisting even at hundreds of picoseconds.

title: Giant Diffusion at Flocking Transitions
summary: We simulate dynamics in two-dimensional aligning active-matter models exhibiting order-disorder transitions in the velocity field. Analysis reveals that the single-particle diffusivity, $D_s$, exhibits strong enhancements at criticality which we quantify via a finite-size scaling method. This dynamical behavior at nonequilibrium flocking transitions is fundamentally different from that at the criticality of equilibrium systems, where diffusivities either vanish or remain non-critical. Furthermore, $D_s$ exhibits pronounced finite-size effects throughout the ordered phase, which also are absent in equilibrium settings. We interpret these counterintuitive transport anomalies within the framework of a flocking theory. Our results suggest that enhanced diffusion generates effective long-range interactions. This relaxes the constraints of the Mermin-Wagner theorem that otherwise prevents order-disorder transitions in two dimensions for systems possessing continuous symmetry. These results are of much experimental relevance and have important implications in formulating quantitative theories for nonequilibrium transports.

title: Attainable and unattainable quantum precision limits in ultrastrong light--matter coupling
summary: In this paper, we study the gauge dependence of quantum precision in ultrastrongly coupled light--matter systems. The unitary between gauges carries the coupling $g$, so each truncation defines a different family. The quantum Fisher information traces an exact parabola across frames. Harmonic matter minimizes it at a universal $\theta_\ast=\Omega/(\Omega+\omega)$, set by the matter and cavity frequencies. Only the minimal-coupling bound is attainable. Frames differ by a factor $9.6$ with opposite trends. Diverging virtual-excitation gain at the Dicke point is a gauge artifact and saturates.

title: Universal two-qubit control across dilution refrigerators via a 10-km coherent optical link
summary: Distributed quantum networks are important for scalable quantum processors and for potential applications in communication, distributed computation, and sensing, in which direct classical links for adaptive control are essential to harness the shared entanglement. However, controlling superconducting quantum processors from a separate refrigerator over long distances remains elusive. Here, we introduce a coherent optical link (COL) that delivers microwave waveforms and their phase references between dilution refrigerators. Combining a laser, a microwave-to-optical transducer and an optical-to-microwave photodiode, the COL transmits microwave control signals over 10~km of fiber, while optical references derived from the same laser compensate for the frequency mismatch between devices. Through the COL, we deliver a universal gate set to a transmon qubit and a cavity qubit in another refrigerator and entangle them, and achieve a Bell-state fidelity of 80.6\%. Quantum control delivered through the COL thus provides a classical backbone for modular quantum processors.

title: Resetting-based designated information distribution
summary: For a network of $n$ nodes under random gossip dynamics, we show that by introducing the additional resetting mechanism (with rate $\beta$) to a designated subset of $r$ nodes, the expected sum of all node values is asymptotically equal to $\tfrac{n}{r}$ times the sum of the initial values of the $r$ designated nodes, in the small-$\beta$ and long-time limit. We also analyze the convergence speed to this asymptotic state and provide an approximate high-probability confidence interval for the expected sum at finite time $t$ and finite $\beta$. Operationally, we propose a protocol that distributes the initial node values over the designated subset evenly (up to a prescribed precision), by appropriately turning on and off the resetting dynamics. Our work not only offers insights into classical problems such as distributed computing and network control, but also serves as a potential foundation for designing quantum algorithms that prepare desired states in quantum networks using only local operations.

title: An Alternative to Quantum Theory
summary: Despite the remarkable empirical success of quantum theory, the interpretation of measurement and the nature of entanglement correlations remain open questions. We outline an alternative framework that seeks to recover the empirical results of quantum theory from a holistic, scale-invariant ontology. Assuming only point particles in Euclidean space, characterised by ratios of masses (and charges) and by the ratios of their mutual separations, the theory describes shapes through a single scale-invariant function; no dynamical evolution is required. In principle, this framework provides a unified description of finite subsystems embedded in a configuration of infinitely many particles and offers a possible route to deriving the observed structures of atoms, molecules and macroscopic bodies without invoking standard quantum mechanics.

title: Holonomy, Spectral Topology, and Detailed Balance in Classical and Open Quantum Systems
summary: Band topology and non-Hermitian spectral theory are now applied to mechanical metamaterials, chiral active fluids, stochastic networks, and open quantum systems. We give a tutorial synthesis organized by holonomy and by one question: what can the spectral data of a linear generator reveal about detailed balance? Three holonomies recur: the Berry phase of a band, the Burgers vector of a dislocation (the integrated torsion of the defect geometry), and the cycle affinity of a Markov network (the holonomy of the connection $\ln(W_{ij}/W_{ji})$). We rederive the Chern numbers $C_m=m(\mathrm{sgn}\,\Omega+\mathrm{sgn}\,\nu_o)$ of a compressible odd-viscous fluid and restate the dislocation zero-mode count of Paulose, Chen, and Vitelli as a pairing of integrated torsion with topological polarization. Our central message is that spectral topology can obstruct detailed balance but does not determine the magnitude of dissipation. Detailed balance is self-adjointness in the inner product fixed by the stationary state, so a non-real eigenvalue, an exceptional point (EP), or a nonzero point-gap winding number of a Markov generator rules it out and forces entropy production $\sigma>0$, with $\sigma\ge k_B j^2/D$ for any current, whereas a real, diagonalizable spectrum does not in general certify it. In the Hatano-Nelson ring, which is normal yet has complex spectrum, $\sigma$ sweeps $(0,\infty)$ at fixed winding number. EPs need a separate assessment of the dynamics: with generalized detailed balance including time-reversal parity, an EP is compatible with equilibrium only through time-reversal-odd dynamics, as at critical damping of a Langevin oscillator, whereas an EP of a system with only even variables, such as an odd elastic medium, certifies a nonequilibrium steady state; in both cases $\sigma$ is analytic across the EP. We propose benchtop tests for each statement.

title: Symanzik Effective Hamiltonian for Lattice Quantum Field Theories
summary: We propose a framework to construct the Symanzik effective Hamiltonian for lattice quantum field theories directly based on dimensional analysis and symmetries in the Hamiltonian formulation. This allows to classify all operators which can contribute at a given order in the spatial lattice spacing. This list can be reduced using the equations of motion and other identities. We exemplify the framework for $\phi^4$ and pure gauge theory, obtaining results consistent with earlier publications for the case of classical improvement. It provides the means to develop a non-perturbative improvement programme in the Hamiltonian formulation of lattice quantum field theories in the future.

title: Singularising quantum channels preserving kappa-additivity
summary:
We construct quantum channels by averaging unitary shift conjugations with respect to $\kappa$-additive probability measures on measurable abelian groups.
 The channels act on the duals of operator algebras generated by shifts and bounded measurable multiplication operators.
 They preserve $\kappa$-additivity of quantum states and admit a weak-$*$ integral representation on this class.
 If the averaging measure vanishes on singletons, every output state is singular.
 In the appendix, we also establish the corresponding Fubini's theorem for $\kappa$-additive measures.

title: Topological states in fractals through a self-similar tensor network encoding
summary: Tensor network methods have been instrumental in addressing exponentially large many-body problems. Most recently, these techniques have also been applied to single-particle tight-binding Hamiltonians, allowing observables to be evaluated on exponentially large lattices. Here, we show that the scale-separated nature of these methods allows for a natural encoding of self-similar structures, such as the Sierpiński gasket, a scale-invariant fractal with Hausdorff dimension $\log 3/\log 2 \approx 1.58$, yielding an exact and compact representation of Hamiltonians on such lattices. Using this encoding, we study a Chern insulator, the flux kagome model, confined to this fractal geometry, and develop methods to investigate its topological states within a tensor network framework. This allows us to reach much higher fractal generations than would otherwise be possible with dense-matrix methods, resolving the density of states of a deep fractal with over 100 million sites. Furthermore, the larger structures allow us to resolve topology in smaller gaps, suggesting that these methods could be instrumental in understanding the interplay between topology and non-integer dimensionality.

title: Memory in biological Lévy walks from the dynamic-entropy formalism
summary: Lévy walks are recognized by the histogram of their flight lengths, while the renewal hypothesis on which the textbook model rests, that every flight is drawn afresh, is seldom tested. We test it with the dynamic-entropy formalism. Maximizing the causal entropy of a sequence of logarithmic flight lengths at fixed lagged correlations yields a chain of continuous spins on a compact interval, whose depth, selected by the data, tells a renewal walker from a Markovian one and from one with a longer memory. With one lag the chain is exactly solvable. A duality that exchanges long and short flights locates a first-order condensation of the flights at the upper cutoff, with the logarithmic range of the flights in the role of system size, and a positive memory makes the histogram heavier-tailed than the rule that generates each flight. For groups, the same construction separates the memory of each individual from delayed interactions and from drives common to all units, which an analysis of the group average confounds, and it gives the collective speed a critical point. On open data, renewal is rejected in seven of ten conditions of Drosophila larvae and in every termite, whose memory reaches a few flights back and lowers the exponent of the histogram by more than half a unit below that of the one-step rule. Wild baboons align with where their nearest neighbors, those ahead above all, were heading 10 to 30 s earlier, and homing pigeons are coupled across their small flocks. Zebrafish T cells, a negative control, remember their own speed, but no delayed coupling between the speeds of different cells survives the controls.

title: Direct imaging of vortex lattices across fractional fillings in two-dimensional Josephson junction arrays
summary: Josephson junction arrays are predicted to host a rich sequence of commensurate vortex lattices. However, direct imaging of these configurations remains limited, while transport measurements cannot resolve the underlying vortex arrangements or how order breaks down. Using scanning superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) microscopy, we resolve individual vortices and directly image this long-predicted hierarchy spanning filling factors $f$ = 1/8 to 1/2 in two-dimensional Au-Nb Josephson junction arrays, including several states with no discernible transport signatures. At $f$ = 1/4, two structurally distinct vortex orders with 4$\times$4 and 2$\times$4 unit cells coexist, consistent with their energetic degeneracy in the frustrated XY model. Away from commensurate filling, we resolve defect structures tied to the underlying vortex-lattice order: the $f$ = 1/2 checkerboard retains its order around isolated excess vortices and vacancies, whereas the $f$ = 1/3 staircase fragments into domains separated by domain walls. These results reveal how frustration, competing configurations, and defects shape the spatial coherence of commensurate vortex order in engineered superconducting lattices.

title: The finite projective classification of complex spinors via momentum maps
summary: We describe the projective orbits of complex spinors from the point of view of the momentum map. We treat the irreducible spin modules in odd dimensions 1,3,5,7,9,11 and the half-spin modules in even dimensions 2,4,6,8,10,12,14, which are the only cases with finitely many orbits. In the Clifford--Fock model, we construct representatives as sums of pure basis spinors, and the coefficients are chosen so that the representative is a critical point of the squared norm of the momentum map. The resulting momentum values in a fixed Weyl chamber distinguish the orbits. Completeness follows from Vinberg's theory of graded Lie algebras and stabilizer actions, independently of the classical spinor classifications. We recover the classical counts of 1,1,1,2,3,5 orbits in the odd cases and 1,1,1,2,2,4,9 in the even cases, and compute the projective dimension of every orbit. In dimension fourteen we also determine the closure order of the orbits, using the fact that the minimum of the squared momentum norm increases strictly under degeneration.

title: Resolving the backbone of multiscale interactions through mutual information rates
summary: Natural systems are often composed of processes evolving on multiple timescales and coupled through complex interaction networks. Inferring such networks is especially challenging when timescales are widely separated, since resolving the fastest processes while accurately sampling the slowest ones is generally prohibitive. In this work, we propose a framework to reconstruct a multiscale interaction tree by combining a rescaled version of the mutual information rate, its conditional counterpart, and the ordering of timescales. We derive an exact theory for stationary Gaussian processes, finding that these measures identify directly connected processes, with the asymptotic mutual information rate distinguishing fast-to-slow from slow-to-fast couplings. We show that this reconstruction can be achieved from the spectral matrix and illustrate its robustness to finite trajectory lengths, moderate timescale separation, and weak nonlinearities. Our work paves the way for exploiting the presence of multiple timescales in real-world systems as a source of structural identifiability rather than an obstacle to network inference.

title: Quotient Index for Symmetry-Protected Zeros and the Tenfold Way in Mackey's Construction of Super Corepresentations
summary: Symmetries that anticommute with a Hamiltonian can protect zero modes by obstructing their removal through symmetry-compatible perturbations. We formulate this obstruction as a quotient of the additive group of symmetry representations by the image of the map that forgets a compatible representation grading. To compute the quotient, we use Mackey's method to construct all irreducible super corepresentations of finite graded symmetry groups, allowing antiunitary operations and projective factor systems. Starting from the unitary Hamiltonian-preserving normal subgroup, this construction yields two complex and ten real structural types, characterized by residual Altland--Zirnbauer symmetry algebras. The residual and induced graded modules have isomorphic graded commutants, and their represented symmetry algebras share a graded Morita class that is super opposite to that of the commutant. We derive character criteria that identify these types. Exhaustive enumeration of the restriction relations gives independent sector contributions $0$, $Z$, or $Z_2$, with only integer factors in the purely unitary case. In the finite semisimple setting, the complete index vanishes if and only if all zero modes can be lifted by a symmetry-compatible perturbation. Applications to one-dimensional end states and interpolation cylinders of disordered boundary Dirac theories recover protected multiplet counts and connect the quotient to bulk topology and sigma-model topological terms using bulk--boundary correspondence, texture-index theorems, and fermion-phase calculations.

title: Contrasting one- and two-particle excitations in cuprate strange metals
summary: In unconventional superconductivity, the pairing mechanism remains one of the central unresolved problems in solid-state physics. Moreover, the normal state shows strong deviations from conventional Fermi-liquid behavior, most notably a scattering rate that is linear in energy and temperature. Here we study the momentum dependence of the energy and damping of collective excitations in optimally doped cuprates in the normal state. In particular, we analyze existing Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (EELS) data of Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8 [Phys. Rev. B 44, 7155 (1991)] and new analogous optical plasmon data of Bi2Sr2Ca2Cu3O10. Furthermore, we reanalyze similar Resonant Inelastic Xray Scattering (RIXS) acoustic plasmon data [Phys. Rev. R 6, 043184 (2024)] of La1.84Sr0.16CuO4 and La1.84Ce0.16CuO4. We contrast these two-particle excitation results with one-particle excitations measured by Angle-Resolved Photoemission Spectroscopy (ARPES). Most of the plasmon behavior can be described well by combined self-energies of a hole and an electron. The dispersion of optical plasmons at high energy is only weakly determined by correlation effects, indicating resilient quasiparticles. The damping of the optical plasmons at low energy, however, is strongly influenced by the reduced scattering rates described in the marginal Fermi liquid model for "strange-metal" behavior. In addition, the same model describes the linear-in-energy damping of acoustic plasmons. Contrary to some theoretical predictions, we see no overdamped optical plasmons below the classical Lindhard critical wave vector.

title: All-to-all connectivity via adiabatic ZZ interactions in a superconducting flux qubit processor
summary: Scalable superconducting quantum processors would benefit from high qubit connectivity, yet existing architectures connect neighbouring qubits via tunable couplers, which introduce substantial wiring and control overhead. Here, we propose a baseband-driven adiabatic ZZ gate that entangles any selected pair in a register of flux qubits coupled via a common cavity. The qubits stay dc-biased at their flux sweet spot. Strong drives applied selectively through local flux lines, at frequencies far below the qubit transitions, adiabatically tilt the quantization axes and generate an effective longitudinal ZZ interaction. The strength of the coupling is tunable and controlled by the amplitudes and relative phase of the drives rather than by any resonance condition. Numerical simulations give coherent gate errors below $10^{-4}$ over broad ranges of drive frequency, with comparable fidelities for two simultaneous gates in a four-qubit register. The protocol is robust against frequency fluctuations and remains effective even when many qubits are coupled to the cavity.

title: Spin-valve effect through electrostatic coupling
summary: We propose a spin-valve effect in which an insulating magnetic van der Waals multilayer controls the conductance of an adjacent non-magnetic conductor by electrostatic coupling, without transport-electrons entering the magnetic layers. The coupling is induced by the variations of the electronic structure when the relative orientation of the magnetization of adjacent monolayers changes from parallel to antiparallel, modifying both the dielectric constant and band alignment. We consider two types of coupling and device concepts: charge transfer to a graphene monolayer and capacitive coupling in a single-electron transistor. We use density functional calculations to assess the magnitude of the effect in various materials, including CrI$_3$, CrBr$_3$, CrCl$_3$ and NiBr$_2$. We predict magnetoresistance ratios in the range of 1.14-1.20 for the charge-transfer device and up to $10^3$ in the single-electron transistor.

title: Long-Range Ergotropy Transfer with Weakened Boundary-Coupling Spin Chains
summary: Ergotropy is a key quantity of a quantum battery that measures the maximum extractable energy. When the extraction process is not local, a faithful transfer of ergotropy across distance is necessary. In this work, we investigate such transfer by using spin chains with weakened coupling at the boundaries as mediator. Weakening the coupling at the two boundaries of the chain gives rise to localized edge states allowing high fidelity transfer within given time duration. We found that, for long spin chains, the transferred ergotropy alternates between even and odd number of spins. We explain this parity effect by investigating the chain spectral structure. Furthermore, we consider both the nearest-neighbor and long-range interactions between spin. In both model of interactions, weakening the boundary couplings improves the maximum transferred ergotropy for long spin chain, compared with in the case of conventional uniform chain. Although the long-range interaction reduces the transferred ergotropy, the transfer time is reduced, too, in particular for longer chain. In addition to the total transferred ergotropy, we also investigate the effect of initial states of the sender spin to the transport of the coherent and incoherent components of the total ergotropy, and the average transport efficiency.

title: Reducing Provers in Distributed Quantum Verification
summary:
In the distributed quantum Merlin-Arthur ($\mathsf{dQMA}$) model introduced by Fraigniaud, Le Gall, Nishimura, and Paz (ITCS 2021), a network of quantum computers verifies a global property with the aid of a quantum proof supplied by an untrusted prover. While the nodes are computationally unbounded, the challenge is to limit proof size and the communication required for verification. In this paper, we consider the model of Hasegawa, Kundu, and Nishimura (PODC 2024), where the proof must be unentangled across nodes, and define its extension to $k$ unentangled provers, denoted by $\mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$. In this setting, we investigate the proof size per node and the communication costs of reducing the number of provers.
 Our first result reduces the number of provers from $k$ to two, doubling the proof size without additional communication. Moreover, with four additional rounds, we can reduce the number of provers from $k$ to one, using at most three times the original local proof size plus a logarithmic term in the number of nodes. Finally, we establish amplification for perfectly complete protocols. In this regime, a single prover suffices with a constant-factor overhead in our reductions, yielding $\mathsf{dQMAS} = \mathsf{dQMAS}(k)$.

title: Effective Time Advance of Quantum Clocks under Postselection
summary: In the familiar twin paradox, the traveling twin ages less than the one who stays behind as a consequence of relativistic time dilation. Here, we show that quantum postselection can effectively reverse this outcome. Using an analytically solvable quantum clock model, we demonstrate that postselection of the center-of-mass motion produces an effective time advance through anomalous weak values, even though every individual motional branch undergoes ordinary time dilation. We extend this analysis to a weak gravitational field and show that an effective time advance can arise even for simple coherent states of the quantum clock motion. We further illustrate this effect using a hydrogen-like atom, revealing how it manifests itself in the atomic wavefunction. Our results demonstrate that quantum interference and postselection can produce an effective time advance beyond conventional relativistic time dilation.

title: Neutronic Field-Effect Transistor
summary: Field-effect electronic devices are in widespread use in communication, computing, data storage, and sensing applications. We demonstrate a neutronic field-effect transistor (NFET) that is analogous to the Datta-Das electron spin transistor and atomtronic devices. The NFET is based on a perfect-crystal Mach-Zehnder neutron interferometer with phase shifts applied to the spin and path degrees of freedom.

title: Compensation Domain Walls in Ferrimagnets as Spin-Torque Oscillator Candidates
summary: Spin-torque nano-oscillators are promising nanoscale microwave sources, yet their performance is often limited by narrow operational ranges and sensitivity to device parameters. Here, we numerically investigate the dynamics of compensation domain walls in ferrimagnetic systems driven by spin-transfer torque as a microwave source candidate. These walls arise in structures with adjacent regions of different compensation character, where the competition between exchange and Zeeman energies under an applied magnetic field stabilizes a distinct magnetic texture. We demonstrate steady current-driven rotation of compensation domain walls over a broad range of current densities within the model. To elucidate the underlying mechanism, we develop a collective-coordinate model and derive an analytical expression for the oscillation frequency, which quantitatively reproduces the dependence on current and magnetic field observed in micromagnetic simulations. Our results identify compensation domain walls as a candidate platform for tunable spin-torque nano-oscillators with intrinsic field-induced confinement.

title: A Hierarchy of Fast and Strong Signatures for Vertex Orbits
summary: The defining features of a physical system are its symmetries and its invariants. For a network, the symmetries are the automorphisms, and the invariants are the vertex orbits they define. Two vertices of a graph may appear structurally indistinguishable without being interchangeable under any graph automorphism. Distinguishing apparent similarity from genuine symmetry lies at the heart of the vertex-orbit partition problem. In this work, we develop a hierarchy of increasingly expressive, automorphism-invariant signatures that draw on the spectral properties of the graph Laplacian and the Dirac operator to reveal subtle structural differences. Guided by a sequence of counterexamples, we progressively strengthen these signatures, ultimately incorporating probing techniques, which are temporary structural perturbations, that expose the hidden distinctions in the original unperturbed graph. We evaluate our approach across diverse benchmark families, recovering exact orbit partitions in challenging instances, including graphs that resist low-dimensional Weisfeiler--Leman refinement. We also examine the computational and numerical limitations of our constructions, distinguishing empirical success from theoretical completeness. Our findings highlight the potential of spectral and probing-based methods for uncovering the structural distinctions that define vertex orbit.

title: Higher tensor network states in two spatial dimensions: fundamental theorem for open boundary conditions
summary: We introduce a class of two-dimensional tensor network states obtained by categorifying matrix product states. This procedure leads us to consider bond spaces provided by a 2-vector space associated with the 2-cells of the underlying lattice. Tensor network representations are then defined as module categories over the free monoidal category on a monoidal signature encoding the lattice geometry. We prove a fundamental theorem stating that two representations generating the same states with suitable open boundary conditions are equivalent as module categories. Finally, we introduce a notion of 2-injectivity, a categorified analogue of the injectivity condition for matrix product states.

title: Ground-state phase diagram of the spin-1/2 Heisenberg zigzag ladder with anisotropic $Γ$ term revisited
summary: We study the spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet with an anisotropic $\Gamma$ term on a zigzag ladder, which can be exactly mapped to the spin-1/2 XYZ zigzag ladder by a spin rotation. This model has recently attracted considerable interest as an effective model for the quasi-one-dimensional magnetic semiconductor YbCuS$_2$. For the model, the ground-state phase diagram was previously proposed by Saito and Hotta [Phys. Rev. Lett. 132, 166701 (2024); Phys. Rev. B 110, 024409 (2024)]. We systematically reexamine the phase diagram through complementary numerical and analytical approaches, including exact diagonalization, the density-matrix renormalization group method, and low-energy effective theories. We thereby demonstrate that when the anisotropic $\Gamma$ term is present, the model exhibits the Néel, dimer, ferromagnetic, and double-Néel phases, all of which have a finite excitation gap. The gapless Tomonaga-Luttinger-liquid (TLL) phase appears only in the isotropic case where the $\Gamma$ term is absent. We also confirm that the transitions between the Néel and dimer phases and between the Néel and ferromagnetic phases are continuous transitions governed by Gaussian criticality with central charge $c=1$. The TLL parameter characterizing the critical states at the Gaussian transitions is estimated numerically.

title: Quantum Residual Exploration for Selected Configuration Interaction
summary: We propose a modular hybrid quantum-classical method to improve selected configuration interaction at a fixed final determinant budget. Quantum measurements supply complementary determinants, accepted only when they outrank classical candidates under a common energetic criterion. This targets multistep excitations that perturbative discovery may miss in strongly correlated systems. A demonstration on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer shows that measured proposals for H$_{12}$ at a stretched geometry lower the variational energy relative to classical-only selection at the same final determinant budget.

title: Renewal Bias in Parallel Simulations of Absorbing Processes
summary: Asynchronous parallel simulations of stochastic processes with absorbing states can exhibit systematic sampling bias when trajectory durations depend on their eventual absorbing outcomes. Workers that continuously restart upon absorption preferentially record rapidly terminating trajectories within a fixed computational budget, distorting the observed ensemble statistics. We investigate this effect using a minimal renewal model with two absorbing states and state-dependent exponential durations. Renewal theory yields exact expressions for the expected number and composition of completed trajectories, showing that the resulting bias decreases algebraically with execution time but persists as the number of parallel workers increases at fixed budget. We compare continuous sampling with First-Trajectory Filtering, which retains only the initial trajectory attempted by each worker. Although finite execution deadlines introduce residual censoring bias, this bias decreases exponentially with the computational budget. An analytical mean-squared error calculation reveals budget-dependent crossover worker allocations beyond which First-Trajectory Filtering becomes more accurate despite collecting fewer trajectories. We also examine the limitations of statistical inference under severe censoring when the absorbing-state probabilities and characteristic durations are unknown. Finally, simulations of the Axelrod model near its nonequilibrium transition demonstrate the preferential sampling of rapidly absorbing fragmented configurations, illustrating the relevance of the renewal mechanism in a spatially interacting system. Our results show that increasing computational throughput does not necessarily improve statistical accuracy and highlight the importance of accounting for trajectory-duration heterogeneity in parallel simulations of absorbing processes.

title: One-Particle Resonances and Eigenstate Thermalization in Periodic Free-Fermion Lattices
summary: We study eigenstate fluctuations of the particle number in the nearest-neighbour free-fermion model on the periodic cubic lattice $(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^d$. For every fixed dimension, every particle number, every subvolume, and every normalized energy eigenstate, we prove a bound of order $NL^{d-1}$ for the particle-number variance. The corresponding eigenstate-thermalization estimate is of order $L^{d-1}/(N\eta^2)$ for fluctuations of relative size $\eta$. In particular, at positive particle density the bound decays as the inverse linear size. The proof decomposes the centered particle-number operator according to one-particle energy transfer and treats the zero- and nonzero-transfer components separately. The nonzero-transfer part is controlled by a sharp resonance bound, proved from Mann's theorem on relations among roots of unity, while the zero-transfer part is estimated by a Hilbert-Schmidt argument. These bounds are optimal in every dimension: the maximal nonzero-gap multiplicity has order $L^{d-1}$, and suitable many-body eigenstates realize matching variance lower bounds and show that the concentration bound cannot be improved in estimates uniform in the tolerance parameter.

title: Polynomial-Space Quantum Algorithms from Classical Branching: Colouring, Domination and Monotone Local Search
summary: We give quantum algorithms for exponential-time problems on $n$ vertices or elements, with bounded error, polynomial space and no quantum random access memory. Our results are these. (1) 4-Colouring in quantum time $O(1.3032^n)$, from a polynomial-space branching algorithm with polynomial-space terminal algorithms; with the branching algorithm alone, $O(1.3100^n)$. The previous best bound in this model, to our knowledge, is $O(1.3231^n)$. (2) $k$-Colouring below the previous best bound for $k \in \{5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11\}$ and $13 \le k \le 18$, from $O(1.4518^n)$ for $k = 5$ to $O(1.9233^n)$ for $k = 18$. (3) Dominating Set in $O(1.2235^n)$, against the previous $O(2^{n/2})$, Independent Dominating Set in $O(1.1583^n)$, and Edge Dominating Set and Minimum Maximal Matching in $O(1.1501^n)$. (4) A quantum form of monotone local search: if the extension problem has a backtracking tree with $c^k$ nodes up to polynomial factors, the problem is solved in quantum time $(2 - 1/c)^{n/2}$ up to polynomial factors. This gives Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3081^n)$, Subset and Group Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3229^n)$, Cluster Vertex Deletion in $O(1.2033^n)$, 3-Hitting Set in $O(1.2405^n)$, Proper Interval Vertex Deletion in $O(1.3541^n)$, Multicut on Trees in $O(1.1647^n)$ and Min-Ones $d$-SAT in $O^*((2-1/d)^{n/2})$. (5) Quantum exponential-time approximations below the quantum exact bounds, such as a 1.1-approximation for Vertex Cover in $O(1.0555^n)$ and for Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.2161^n)$. The colouring exponents for $k \ge 6$ come from an evaluation of a known reduction recursion, computed in floating point with a margin.

title: No Exponential Quantum Advantage for Decoded Quantum Interferometry with Local Quantum Decoders
summary: Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) reduces optimization of sparse linear constraint problems, and sampling from their Gibbs measures, to decoding a linear code from a quantum state. We study DQI on random $D$-regular $k$-sparse instances with $k\ge3$, for which local decoders such as belief propagation with quantum messages (BPQM) are commonly used. Such decoders estimate a typical codeword symbol using only the qudits within logarithmic distance of it. Our main insight is that the thresholds of the decoding problem induced by DQI correspond to phase transitions of the Gibbs measure that are well studied in statistical physics: tree reconstruction for local decoders and, for Max-$k$-XORSAT, condensation for the optimal decoder. This insight allows us to prove two main results. First, we prove an information-theoretic obstruction: no local decoder can recover the codeword with high probability above the tree reconstruction threshold. Conversely, we show that a decoder based on BPQM reaches this threshold. Since the cavity method predicts that local Markov chains equilibrate rapidly up to the same threshold, we expect DQI with local decoders to give no exponential speedup for sampling and no advantage in approximate optimization with amplitude functions that depend only on the number of violated constraints. Second, we consider the optimal decoder (the pretty-good measurement, for which no efficient implementation is known) and show that it succeeds exactly below the condensation threshold. The condensation threshold thus provides a tight upper bound on the performance of DQI with these amplitude functions, providing a strict refinement of the limit that Jordan et al.\ derived from the Holevo bound. Our results point to efficient nonlocal decoders that succeed between the two thresholds as the only viable path to a quantum advantage with DQI on these instances.

title: Spin Shuttling Through Quantum-Dot Based Chiral Molecular Bridges: Gauge Constraints, Holonomy, and Quantum Gates
summary: Chiral molecular bridges between silicon quantum dots can provide novel two-qubit entangling resources via the chirality-induced spin-selectivity (CISS) effect. We evaluate this using Makhlin invariants. Modeling a phase-coherent bridge as an $\mathrm{SU}(2)$-valued hopping between two spins, a Schrieffer-Wolff reduction yields a twisted exchange interaction $J \mathbf{S}_1 \cdot \mathbf{R} \mathbf{S}_2$, whose Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya and symmetric anisotropic parts are fixed by a single bridge angle $\alpha$. Using the Kaplan-Shekhtman-Entin-Wohlman-Aharony (KSEA) gauge argument, we prove this interaction is locally equivalent to isotropic exchange; thus, a single chiral bond does not constitute a new entangling class. Breaking this gauge symmetry reveals genuine chiral utility: chiral exchange converts a uniform transverse field into a synthetic gradient, bringing the two-qubit propagator within $7\times10^{-4}$ of the CNOT class in invariant space 4.7 times faster than an equivalent orthogonal gradient. Shuttling a spin through bridges with non-collinear axes implements a non-Abelian $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ holonomy, yielding rotationally non-reciprocal transport and closed-loop geometric gates that suppress dynamical-phase noise to second order. To address the unsettled microscopic origin of CISS, we introduce a unified transport channel combining coherent rotation, a direction-reversing spin filter, and pointer-basis dephasing. This model obeys an exact $\tanh$ composition law for pumped polarization and a closed-form transverse decay law, yielding four observables that experimentally over-determine the bridge's coherent fraction $F_c$. Finally, we quantify silicon-specific hardware constraints, establishing the Landau-Zener valley-adiabaticity window ($E_v \geq 2.1\sqrt{\hbar v}$) and charge-noise limit ($\sigma_J/J \leq 3\%$) required for $99\%$ gate fidelity.

title: Quantum Robustness via Sandwiched Rényi Divergences
summary: If a quantum state is known only approximately, how much can the expectation of an observable change? We answer with the worst-case expectation over all states within a sandwiched Rényi divergence budget of a reference state, for every order $\alpha \in [1/2,\infty]$. Convex duality gives this value as a one-dimensional optimization over a sandwiched Schatten norm, running from a fidelity risk at $\alpha = 1/2$, through the entropic risk at $\alpha = 1$, to a quantum conditional value-at-risk at $\alpha = \infty$. The main result is a classicalization theorem: the quantum problem coincides with the classical one for a probability measure $\omega_\alpha$ on the spectral interval of the observable, constructed from Heinävaara's tracial joint spectral measure and given by Stahl's theorem at $\alpha = 1$. The Hoeffding, Bernstein and Markov--Krein bounds of classical probability thereby apply to the quantum problem, and yield Pinsker-type inequalities with Bernstein-type refinements. The measure $\omega_\alpha$ is the Born measure only at $\alpha = 1/2$; for $\alpha > 1/2$, noncommutativity of the observable with the state strictly lowers its variance below the Born variance, and with it every variance-sensitive bound: a quantum deflation.

title: $\mathsf{EQP}\subseteq\mathsf{IP}$ Does Not Relativize
summary: We construct a recursive oracle $O$ and a unary language $L\in\mathsf{EQP}^O\setminus(\mathsf{IP}^O\cup\mathsf{PH}^O)$, strengthening the $\mathsf{BQP}$ versus $\mathsf{IP}$ oracle separation of Bouland et al. to exact quantum computation. The separation is based on a variant of the Forrelation problem in which the normalized correlation of one Boolean function with the Fourier transform of another is promised to be exactly $+1/2$ or $-1/2$. The main technical contribution is a repair method that constructs distributions supported on these exact levels while preserving the indistinguishability needed for the $\mathsf{IP}$ and $\mathsf{PH}$ lower bounds. A uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm distinguishes the two cases with certainty using only three oracle queries.

title: Global Asymptotics of a Toda Soliton Condensate with Random Scattering Data
summary: We study a dense $N$-soliton condensate for the infinite Toda lattice in the limit $N \to \infty$. In contrast to previous mathematical studies of soliton gases where the norming constants are assumed to be deterministic or infinitesimal, we consider initial scattering data where both the discrete eigenvalues and the norming constants are independent random variables. The norming constants $\gamma_j$ are allowed to be arbitrarily large under a mild moment condition $\mathbb{E}[\gamma_j^\nu] < \infty$ ($\nu > 1$). Our main result is divided into two parts. First, we develop a probabilistic Riemann--Hilbert framework to show that the system self-averages: despite large, independent fluctuations in the initial data, the random Toda lattice variables converge deterministically to an effective continuum model at a polynomial rate $\mathcal{O}(N^{-\delta})$ for $0 < \delta < 1/2$. Second, by performing the Deift--Zhou nonlinear steepest descent analysis of the continuum problem, we obtain the complete leading-order macroscopic description of the lattice across the entire space-time plane. The solution decomposes into five distinct finite-gap regimes, characterized explicitly by modulated elliptic and genus-2 waves with an error of order $\mathcal{O}(1/\ln N)$. In contrast to the straight characteristic rays typical of standard soliton gas limits, the interfaces separating these five macroscopic regimes in the space-time plane are genuinely non-linear curves; in particular, the boundary of the modulated genus-2 region is completely non-linear. Finally, under our assumptions, we establish the Nonlinear Dispersion Relations for the Toda soliton condensate and prove that the macroscopic ensemble averages are determined by the soliton gas density of states.

title: Sequential vs parallel Strategies for Sharing Quantum Advantage in Communication Tasks
summary: Information can be extracted from a quantum system in a sustainable manner, allowing the system to be reused for further information extraction through subsequent interactions. We investigate the possibility of consensus between two experimentally feasible methods, namely, parallel and sequential sharing, that enable multiple observers to extract information encoded in a quantum system. We show that any statistics generated by a parallel sharing strategy can be reproduced by a sequential strategy when only two observers are involved. However, when more than two observers participate in sharing quantum correlations, certain statistics achievable through parallel strategies cannot be reproduced by sequential strategies. Moreover, we demonstrate that sharing quantum advantage through a parallel strategy is impossible for a class of communication tasks involving two decoding measurements, thereby establishing an arbitrarily large gap between the sustainability of quantum advantage under sequential and parallel strategies. This naturally raises the question of whether this impossibility extends to communication tasks involving more than two decoding measurements. We show that, while parallel sharing of quantum advantage is impossible in a 3-bit random access code (RAC), it becomes possible in a 3-bit parity-oblivious RAC, where at most two observers can simultaneously obtain a quantum advantage by performing measurements on two imperfect clones of the initially prepared quantum system. Our findings have potential applications in the development of quantum communication networks and distributed quantum information processing.

title: Succinct Infinite-Horizon Lyapunov and LQR Value Problems Are BQP-Complete
summary: Fundamental tasks in linear systems analysis and control require evaluating infinite-horizon output energies for autonomous systems and optimal value functions for controlled systems. These quantities are characterized by Lyapunov and algebraic Riccati equations, respectively. In this work, we study promise problems for their evaluation when the system matrices are sparse and represented succinctly by Boolean circuits specifying their nonzero entries, with input length polynomial in the logarithm of the system dimension. For dissipative autonomous systems with coordinate-vector initial states, we define the succinct Lyapunov value problem (SLV). Its extension to linear-quadratic optimal control is the succinct LQR value problem (SLQRV). We prove that SLV is $\BQP$-hard: every problem in bounded-error quantum polynomial time ($\BQP$) reduces to it in polynomial time. We then establish that the more general SLQRV problem admits a quantum algorithm running in time polynomial in the succinct input length. Since SLV is a special case of SLQRV, both problems are $\BQP$-complete. Consequently, unless bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time coincides with $\BQP$, no classical randomized algorithm can solve either problem on all promised instances in time polynomial in the succinct input length.

title: An efficient classical algorithm for OTOCs in chaotic quantum dynamics
summary: Estimating out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in individual instances of random quantum circuits has been proposed as a candidate for verifiable quantum advantage, and demonstrated to be hard for conventional classical algorithms such as tensor networks and Monte Carlo. Using insights from quantum chaos, we develop and implement a polynomial-time classical algorithm for the four-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and the eight-point ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in typical instances of one-dimensional (1D) quantum circuits. Our results demonstrate average-case classical tractability of estimating OTOCs in the sensitive regime where circuit-to-circuit fluctuations are large. Our algorithm organizes the OTOC into a rapidly converging series, where the leading term includes contributions from histories within permutation degrees of freedom in the replicated Hilbert space, and subleading terms arise from excursions outside this space. Although chaos is often viewed as an insurmountable barrier to classical simulation, our algorithm exploits a form of dephasing caused by chaos, which suppresses the subleading terms. We provide strong theoretical and numerical evidence to support this suppression. Further, we demonstrate that practical implementations of our algorithm estimate ${\rm OTOC}^{(1)}$ and ${\rm OTOC}^{(2)}$ in 1D circuits with high accuracy, achieving higher signal-to-noise ratio at larger circuit depths compared to recent 2D experiments by Google. Extending our algorithm to higher dimensions, and resolving the status of quantum advantage in 2D OTOCs, remain open problems.

title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
summary: We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

title: Self-Energy Construction for Chain Representations of Open Quantum Systems
summary: We identify the self-energy as the environmental response to the system, which transforms covariantly under shifts of the system--environment cut. For a semi-infinite chain with asymptotically uniform parameters, this transformation admits a fixed point that defines the asymptotic boundary self-energy (BSE), whose spectral density is the Wigner semicircle. A chain-extended BSE exploits the trend of the retained chain, offering improved accuracy in representing the environment. The transformation introduces a pseudo-hyperbolic self-energy distance that is invariant under shifts of the cut, providing a natural geometry for comparing environmental responses. As a demonstration, this geometry enables cut-independent error measure of finite damped-oscillator closures of the chain, distinguishing the closure error from the chain depth error, and offers a more accurate fitting scheme than fitting the time-domain correlation function.

title: Universal semiclassical drift velocity of magnetic edge channels
summary: Magnetic edge channels, arising at the edge of a two-dimensional electron gas in a magnetic field, are topologically protected and propagate unidirectionally along the edge. Their group velocities at the Fermi level, being averaged harmonically, result in drift velocity, which is related to the edge density of states, quantum capacitance, and the velocity of edge magnetoplasmons. Using semiclassical quantization of electron skipping orbits, we show that the drift velocity equals 1/2 of the electron Fermi velocity in the limit of a large number of edge channels crossing the Fermi level. This result, being universal for a hard edge and for isotropic dispersion, is checked numerically for massive electrons and for massless electrons in graphene. The drift velocity at smooth electrostatically defined edges lacks such universality. In the case of anisotropic dispersion, the semiclassical drift velocity at the hard edge reduces to a coordinate-velocity correlation along the cyclotron orbit.

title: Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications
summary: We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the Choi-Kraus operator-sum representation and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems. We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup. This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references. The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.

title: Ambient-pressure superconductivity in bulk single crystals of La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{10}$
summary: Superconductivity in the Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates has so far been confined either to multilayer compounds under high pressure or to square-planar infinite-layer-type films stabilized by epitaxial strain. Here we report the high-pressure high-temperature (HPHT) growth of bulk single crystals of the quadruple-layer RP nickelate La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{13}$ ($n=4$) and reproduce the quintuple-layer La$_6$Ni$_5$O$_{16}$ ($n=5$) synthesis, two members of the series that had previously been accessible only as thin films. Topotactic reduction of La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{13}$ single crystals with CaH$_2$ yields the square-planar phase La$_5$Ni$_4$O$_{10}$, which we show to be a bulk, ambient-pressure superconductor with $T_\mathrm{c}^\mathrm{onset} \approx 18\,\mathrm{K}$, a shielding fraction above 60\%, and a specific-heat jump that confirms a bulk pairing transition. All crystals show besides superconductivity a coexistence with a density-wave or metal-insulator transition. The upper critical field shows a small anisotropy, $\gamma \approx 2.4$, which remains finite as $T \to T_c$, indicating three-dimensional superconductivity with substantial coupling between the four-layer blocks. These results identify the square-planar nickelates $R_{n+1}$Ni$_n$O$_{2n+2}$ as a bulk platform in which the layer number alone tunes the nickel valence into the superconducting regime, without chemical substitution, pressure, or epitaxial constraint.

title: A short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture via the completion framework
summary:
We give a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. If a partial Boolean function $f$ is defined on a $\delta$-fraction of all $n$-bit strings and have quantum query complexity $Q(f)$, then, for every $0<\epsilon<1$, a deterministic algorithm computes $f$ correctly on at least a $1-\epsilon$ fraction of its domain using $O( Q(f)^6 / (\epsilon \delta)^2)$ queries. Our proof uses the completion framework and establishes a more general bound in terms of the classical adversary measure. The only result we use from Turturean's recent proof is a special case of his certificate inequality, for which we provide a self-contained proof.
 We also derive the stronger variant of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture, the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture, from our main result in the appendix.

title: GARI++: A General-Purpose Decoder for Quantum Error Correction
summary: We present GARI++, a two-stage decoding pipeline achieving accuracy competitive with the state of the art across surface, bivariate bicycle and color codes without relying on ensembles. The first stage uses GARI, a normalized min-sum decoder with random serial scheduling on the GARI transformed matrix. The second stage decoder is used only for the cases that the first stage does not converge, and the decoder is configurable based on the choice of the QEC code. The first stage pipelines towards the second stage both the residual syndrome and the soft information. GARI++ pipelining is predictive, meaning that GARI++ chooses the first stage iteration outputs which are expected to deliver the best accuracy in the second stage. GARI++ motivates a hybrid FPGA-CPU architecture for real-time decoding. For example, under uniform circuit-level depolarising noise with a physical error rate of 0.001, the FPGA implementation of GARI achieves average latencies per round ranging from $201 ns$ to $11.8\mu s$ for surface code distances between 7 and 25. At the same time, due to the very low weight residuals output by the first stage, the average residual decoding time per round remains near constant and below one microsecond on a single Apple M2 core for surface code distances even up to 51 when using Union-Find and accuracy on par with correlated MWPM.

title: Property F implies weak integrality for non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion categories
summary: We prove that every non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion category with property F is pseudo-unitary and weakly integral. In particular, every modular category with property F is weakly integral. Neither sphericality nor pseudo-unitarity is assumed. Passing to the Drinfeld centre extends the result to degenerate categories whose dimensions are positive on the intersection of the Müger centre with the adjoint subcategory; these include every braided fusion category with a pseudo-unitary Galois conjugate. Physically, the result connects the arithmetic of topological orders to the computational power of anyon braiding: non-integer squared total quantum dimension guarantees infinite braid group images, a necessary condition for universal quantum computation.

title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
summary: Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of $\mu \text{eV}$ in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.

title: The hidden symmetry operators of the asymmetric quantum Rabi model and its two-photon and two-mode variants in closed form
summary: The asymmetric quantum Rabi model, a two-level system with splitting $\Delta$ and bias $\epsilon$ coupled with strength $g$ to a boson mode, has level crossings when $\epsilon$ is an integer multiple $N$ of the mode frequency. They are due to a hidden symmetry operator $J$, for which no general formula has been available. Here we obtain $J$ in closed form for every $N$. We find that $J$ is given by the parity of the symmetric model times the continuant (ordered tridiagonal determinant) of $N$ first-order operators, which are the Hamiltonians at the intermediate biases $N-1,N-3,\dots,1-N$ minus a common number operator. The symmetry is thus a staircase of $N$ bias steps that closes on the mirror image of the model precisely at integer bias. The proof uses induction on two commutation relations. The same relations hold in the asymmetric two-photon and two-mode models, written with the generators of $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$, so that the same continuant gives their symmetry operators for every order, previously known only for the lowest ones. We also relate the closed formula for $J$ to the known recursion relations for its coefficients and give their terms of lowest order in $\Delta$ explicitly.

title: Tetragonal-to-orthorhombic distortion in CeRh$_{2}$As$_{2}$
summary: CeRh$_{2}$As$_{2}$ is best known for its two superconducting phases, which are observed when a magnetic field is applied along the $c$ axis of its tetragonal unit cell. The emergence of superconductivity, with $T_{c} \approx 0.31$K, is preceded by an ordered state (phase I), with an ordering temperature $T_{0} \approx 0.46$K. The precise nature of the order parameter in phase I is still unknown, although evidence of dipolar ordering was found. To investigate a possible symmetry breaking at $T_{\textrm{0}}$, we conducted longitudinal thermal-expansion measurements along the crystallographic [100], [010], [110], and [1$\overline{1}$0] directions on a single-crystalline sample cut into an octagonal shape. Our results demonstrate the breaking of the fourfold in-plane symmetry below $T_{\textrm{0}}$, evidencing a small tetragonal-to-orthorhombic distortion (orthorhombicity $\delta \sim 10^{-7}$). The breaking of the tetragonal symmetry at $T_{\textrm{0}}$ might imply that the superconducting order parameter that develops within phase I cannot be multi-component. More generally, the distortion places restrictions on the possible order parameters for phase I.

title: The simulability frontiers of photonic quantum computing
summary: Estimates of when photonic devices outgrow classical simulation are hard to compare: even for single-photon boson sampling, quoted thresholds range from 50 to 98 photons, as they rest on different tasks and assumptions. We propose as a common unit the time a classical computer needs to draw one sample from the device's exact output distribution, up to floating-point rounding. Only exactness applies equally to every kind of light, since the cost of approximate sampling depends on the accuracy required. The simulability frontier is the device size at which our fastest exact sampler produces one sample per second on a fixed machine; this device size increases with better hardware and algorithms. As the time per sample grows exponentially with the number of detected photons, doubling the machine speed moves the frontier by about one photon, whereas a better algorithm changes the growth rate. We measure the frontier with photonic-engines, an open-source GPU library of exact samplers for single photons, entangled photons from quantum emitters, vacuum-single-photon superpositions and squeezed light. Each sampler is validated against a simulator sharing no code with it. On one NVIDIA H100 GPU, with Haar-random interferometers, twice as many modes as photonic inputs and photon-number-resolving detectors, the frontier lies at 38.3 single photons and at 31.0 entangled photons from one emitter. For squeezed light, a timing model fitted to measurements places it at 41.5 squeezed photonic inputs of mean photon number 0.5. For our samplers, coherence alone makes simulation harder: sources that emit a photon with probability one half reach 64.2 when vacuum and photon are mixed incoherently, as for lossy single photons, but only 50.0 when they are in coherent superposition. Feed-forward from mid-circuit measurement of up to three modes lowers the single-photon frontier only from 38.3 to 38.1.

title: Chiral waveguide model for error-correctable quantum computation
summary: We develop a first-principles framework connecting microscopic waveguide scattering to quantum error correction and algorithmic performance. For polarization-encoded single photons interacting with an ensemble of two-level atoms in a chiral waveguide, we derive an effective polarization quantum channel by tracing out the frequency degree of freedom. Using this channel as the physical noise model for a rotated planar code, we observe threshold behavior as the number of atoms $N$ and the atom-waveguide coupling strength $\Gamma$ are varied. An asymptotic analysis of the microscopic scattering model explains the threshold scaling with $N\Gamma/\sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the photon spectral bandwidth. For identical, lossless atoms with symmetric real coupling and a photon spectrum centered at resonance, the effective noise is strongly biased toward $X$ errors. We then incorporate the resulting logical errors into quantum phase estimation and demonstrate that the noise bias can guide circuit design. In particular, a Hadamard-basis implementation reduces sensitivity to the dominant error, improving algorithmic performance.

title: Dephasing-Induced Melting of Crystalline Spectral Form Factors
summary: Long-range spectral order can be probed using spectral form factors, where it manifests itself as sharp Bragg peaks at integer multiples of the Heisenberg time in nearly crystalline spectra. We examine how energy dephasing in open systems affects this spectral order and how to control it. We find that Bragg peaks fade algebraically with revival order and dephasing strength, $K_{\rm Bragg}(p)\propto(\gamma p)^{-1/2}$, within an extensive intermediate regime, and persist up to the lifetime of nearest-neighbor coherences despite an extreme decoherence rate. Our results establish the spectral form factor as a probe of spectral order in open quantum systems and identify temporal correlations in spectral fluctuations as a means of controlling it.
